summary: The paper introduces CODEC, which applies sparse autoencoder decomposition to gradient-based hidden-neuron *contributions* (rather than activations), and reports that contributions are sparser, higher-dimensional, and progressively sign-decorrelated across depth in ResNet-50, with follow-up analyses on ViT-B and retinal CNN models. The contribution-vs-activation framing is a genuinely useful conceptual distinction, and the perturbation (ablation/preservation) experiments provide real causal evidence that contribution modes identify functionally relevant channels better than activation modes. However, the submission is weakened by thin statistical reporting (no seeds, error bars, or significance tests anywhere in the main text), a narrow empirical footprint (essentially one CNN, one ViT with admittedly weaker results, one retinal model), missing engagement with the recent mechanistic-interpretability/SAE literature, and a causal framing that outruns what attribution methods actually establish. This is promising work that needs a substantially more rigorous experimental section before it meets the ICLR bar.
strengths: Clear conceptual contribution: decomposing *contributions* (receptive field x projective field) rather than activations is a well-motivated distinction, and the paper articulates why activation-based analysis cannot answer causal questions.

Causal validation via intervention: the ablation/preservation experiments (Fig. 6) directly test whether contribution modes identify necessary/sufficient channels, which is exactly the right kind of evidence for the paper's central claim and is more convincing than purely correlational interpretability analyses.

Interesting empirical findings: progressive sparsity increase, positive/negative contribution decorrelation across depth, and higher contribution dimensionality are non-obvious observations that could stimulate follow-up work.

Cross-domain applicability demonstrated: image CNNs, a Vision Transformer, and CNN models of retinal ganglion cell responses, with the retina application yielding concrete, experimentally testable hypotheses about interneuron combinations and dynamic receptive fields.
Honest reporting of the ViT weakness: the authors explicitly state that ablation performance was inferior on ViTs and motivate further work on spatial reduction strategies.

key_concerns.issue: No statistical rigor anywhere in the main text: no seeds, error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests for any quantitative claim (sparsity trends, decorrelation across depth, class-correlation of modes, ablation/preservation performance). Key curves (Fig. 5D, Fig. 6D-E) appear to be single-run point estimates, and the perturbation experiments use an unspecified random subsample of the validation set. For a paper whose central claim is that contribution modes are *better* than activation modes, the absence of variance estimates makes the improvement impossible to certify.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Report all quantitative results over multiple SAE training seeds and multiple data subsamples with error bars; add paired statistical tests (e.g., per-class paired comparisons of contribution- vs activation-guided perturbation across all 1000 classes); state sample sizes for every subsampled analysis.

key_concerns.issue: Insufficient baselines for the core claim. The only comparisons are SAE-on-activations and random channel selection. There is no comparison to other channel/neuron selection or circuit-discovery methods (e.g., TCAV-style concept vectors, network dissection, gradient/activation-based channel importance rankings, or simple per-channel contribution ranking without any SAE). It is plausible that much of the perturbation advantage comes from using contributions at all, not from the SAE decomposition into modes.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a 'raw contribution ranking' baseline (top channels by per-class contribution, no SAE) and at least one established alternative (e.g., activation magnitude or gradient-based importance) to isolate what the decomposition itself buys.

key_concerns.issue: Causal language is overclaimed. Integrated Gradients contributions are attributions under a specific baseline and path, not 'direct causal measures'; the paper repeatedly asserts causality (title, 'direct causal measure', 'causal processes that cannot be determined by analyzing activations alone') while the actual causal evidence is limited to the channel-level perturbation experiments on one architecture family. IG with 10 integration steps to the top logit is also a coarse approximation whose sensitivity to step count and baseline choice is not analyzed.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Scope the causal claims to what the perturbation experiments establish; add sensitivity analyses over IG step count, baseline, and contribution target; soften title/abstract language or back it with broader interventional evidence.

key_concerns.issue: Weak positioning against the modern mechanistic interpretability literature. Sparse autoencoders for decomposing network internals are now a large, active area (dictionary learning / SAE feature work in transformers, feature visualization, circuit analysis), yet the prose engages mainly with saliency methods and older CNN-interpretability work. The novelty claim ('contribution modes as a unit of analysis') cannot be evaluated without a fair account of this adjacent work.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a proper related-work section covering SAE/dictionary-learning interpretability, feature visualization, and circuit-level analysis, and delineate precisely what is new: applying SAEs to per-input contribution vectors rather than activations.

key_concerns.issue: Limited breadth relative to the generality claimed. Findings rest on a single CNN (ResNet-50), a single ViT with admittedly inferior results and an acknowledged ad-hoc token-as-space reduction, and one retinal CNN family; the LLM analysis is deferred to an unseen supplement. Claims about 'how nonlinear computations evolve across hierarchical layers' and biological relevance are drawn from one or two instances per claim.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Replicate the layerwise trends (sparsity, decorrelation, dimensionality) and perturbation results on at least 2-3 additional architectures (e.g., VGG, ResNet-18/101, a second ViT size); either include the LLM scaling results in the main text or remove the claim.

key_concerns.issue: Internal inconsistencies and missing methodological detail: training is described as both '~200 epochs' and '300 epochs'; the threshold 0.9 is called the baseline yet Supplementary results say R2 degrades at threshold 0.9 vs 0.5; the size of the 'randomly sampled' validation subset for perturbation experiments is never given; the encoder architecture (MLP size) is referenced only via failure modes.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Reconcile epoch counts, specify all architecture and data-subset details in a single consolidated methods table, and clarify which hyperparameters were used for which figure.

key_concerns.issue: Presentation issues: journal-style (magazine) sectioning rather than standard ICLR structure, several typos ('retinl', 'selecte', 'non-labled'), and garbled equation rendering in the contribution-mapping section that obscures the exact definition of A and C.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Restructure into standard Method/Experiments sections, proofread, and typeset the contribution-mapping equations cleanly with all symbols defined.

questions_for_authors: How many SAE training seeds and data subsamples underlie Figs. 3, 5, and 6, and what is the variance of the contribution-vs-activation perturbation gap across classes and seeds?
Does the perturbation advantage survive when compared against simply ranking channels by raw per-class contribution (no SAE)? What specifically does the decomposition into modes add?

How sensitive are the reported trends (sparsity increase, sign decorrelation, dimensionality) to the IG approximation: number of integration steps, baseline choice, and contribution target (top logit vs top-k vs entropy)?
Why is a hard threshold of 0.9 the baseline when your own robustness analysis indicates it sits near a regime that degrades reconstruction R2?

For the retina results, the claim that modes 'generate experimentally testable hypotheses' is intriguing but untested here — can you provide any validation against held-out interneuron recordings or known retinal circuitry beyond the correlation argument from prior work?

The decorrelation of positive and negative contributions is a headline finding; can you rule out that it is a mechanical consequence of increasing sparsity or of the top-logit target rather than a computational phenomenon?
calibration_check: Partially miscalibrated: the limitations section and the candid ViT discussion are commendable, but the title, abstract, and repeated 'direct causal measure' language claim causal and cross-domain generality that the single-architecture, attribution-based evidence does not yet support.

significance.justification: Contribution modes are a potentially useful unit of analysis and the perturbation results would interest the interpretability community, but impact is capped until the advantage over simpler baselines and other architectures is established.

novelty.justification: Applying SAE decomposition to per-input contribution vectors rather than activations is a genuine and well-motivated twist, though each ingredient (IG attributions, SAEs, channel ablation) is established and the combination is evolutionary.

rigor.justification: The method is reasonable and the interventional validation is the right idea, but causal claims rest on attribution heuristics, key baselines are missing, and several confounds (sparsity-driven decorrelation, IG approximation error) are unaddressed.

statistical_soundness.justification: No seeds, error bars, sample sizes, or significance tests appear anywhere in the main text; all headline quantitative claims are single-run point estimates.

calibration_honesty.justification: A real limitations section and honest ViT reporting are offset by overclaimed causality in the title/abstract and broad generality language unsupported by the evidence.

clarity.justification: The overall narrative is readable and the framework is well explained, but garbled equations in the contribution-mapping section, typos, and inconsistent hyperparameter reporting hurt precision.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows a journal/magazine format (no distinct Related Work, Method, or Experiments sections) rather than standard ICLR structure, though all expected content is present somewhere.

reproducibility.justification: Core hyperparameters (threshold, dictionary size, learning rate, batch size, IG steps, dataset) are given, but contradictory epoch counts, unspecified data subsampling, and missing encoder architecture details would impede exact reproduction.

related_work.justification: Saliency and retina-modeling work is cited, but the large recent literature on SAE-based mechanistic interpretability, feature visualization, and circuit analysis is essentially absent, leaving the novelty claim under-positioned.

figure_quality.justification: Captions describe figures that are well matched to the claims (pipeline schematic, layerwise trend quantification, perturbation dose-response curves, retina IRF analysis) and would genuinely support the argument.

breadth_generality.justification: One CNN, one ViT with admittedly weaker results and an ad-hoc reduction, and one retinal model family, with LLM results deferred to an unseen supplement — insufficient to support the cross-architecture and biological generality claimed.

overall_recommendation.justification: Borderline reject: a promising, well-motivated framework with the right kind of interventional validation, but it needs statistical rigor, stronger baselines, broader replication, and honest scoping of causal claims before acceptance.
